name: David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust
label: Sheldrick Elephants
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Sheldrick Wildlife Trust'.
notes: Orphaned baby elephants at feeding time.

text.description:
The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust is an elephant orphanage and wildlife rehabilitation project inside Nairobi National Park. Dame Daphne Sheldrick founded it in 1977 to honour her late husband, David, a naturalist and the founding warden of Tsavo East National Park. It was known as the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust until it changed its name in February 2019 to honour both of them. Orphaned calves are rescued from across Kenya and brought here to be raised, and later returned to the wild.

It photographs well because the animals come to you. Keepers bring the young elephants up to a rope line, so a phone can get sharp close-ups without any long zoom. Expect calves rolling in the mud and orphans walking into the viewing area, with keepers leading them to the rope, which gives plenty of lively moments. The reddish mud and the keepers' work clothes add colour to the frame.

The public can visit for one hour each day, so the window is short. Arrive early, stay behind the rope and keep your phone ready. Switch the flash off and look after your battery, because you will want to shoot for the whole hour. If you want a second angle, try the spot where the calves play in the mud and the keepers lead them to the rope. Entry is likely to be ticketed and booking may be needed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Trust's elephant orphanage is inside Nairobi National Park, in Nairobi, Kenya.
text.directions_text: Start from central Nairobi and head to the Trust's elephant orphanage in Nairobi National Park. Ask for the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust by name. From the phone icon on the map, the Trust's main site is to the north-east, about 3 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for wide shots of keepers, calves and the rope line together. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for close-up portraits of the elephants as they arrive. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is only worth trying if the group comes very close.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Once in the viewing area, stand on the left-hand side as you walk in. One guide says the elephants usually make their entrance on this side, so you can photograph the orphans approaching, framed by the rope and the keepers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep an elephant on one third of the frame, with a keeper or the rope line giving context. Shoot the calves as they walk in, then step back to the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. For a different view, take a shot of the calves playing in the mud and being led up to the rope line.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn the flash off, as guides advise none here. Tap the elephant to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so dark skin and bright sky keep their detail. Try Live Photos or motion mode to catch calves rolling and splashing. A tripod is not needed with a phone.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The public visit is only about an hour a day, so arrive early to get a good place at the rope and be ready when the elephants enter.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed wildlife site open to the public for one hour a day, so check the official site before you go for times, booking and the current entry price.

name: Nairobi National Park
label: Nairobi National Park
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21601065: large area 'Nairobi National Park' (25858 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Wildlife park with the city skyline behind.

text.description: Nairobi National Park is a wildlife reserve on the edge of a capital city, which is the main reason it is such a good place for photographs. Open grass plain, scattered acacia bushes and, on a clear day, wide sky make easy backdrops for animal pictures. It opened in 1946 and was the first national park in Kenya. It covers about 117 square kilometres and lies roughly 7 km from the centre of Nairobi. The park is fenced on three sides, but the southern edge along the Mbagathi River is open, so wildlife can move between the park and the plains beyond. It is known as one of Kenya's most successful rhino sanctuaries, and the list of animals includes lion, giraffe, zebra, buffalo and hippo. Up to 500 bird species have been recorded here too. Wildlife gathers in the park in the dry season, when the small dams along the river hold water, so that is when you are most likely to see animals. The park is a large area, so treat this spot as a starting place rather than a single view. Animals are usually far away, so use the zoom, and keep a little of the open landscape in the frame to show where you were. Always follow park staff instructions and never leave your vehicle to get closer to an animal.
text.geographic_location: In the south of Nairobi, about 7 km from the city centre, where the city meets open grassland. The park's southern boundary is the Mbagathi River.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Nairobi city centre, which is about 7 km north of the park, and travel south by taxi or hired scooter. Check the official park site for the entrance to use and any rules on moving around inside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for animals, since they are often at a distance. Switch to the default lens (1x) for plains with trees, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) for big sky and wide landscapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Impala Viewpoint (hilltop near the Main Gate, on the highest point). A wide view across the central plains with impalas, zebras and gazelles grazing below and the Nairobi skyline in the distance. From here you look across towards the open park area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the lower or upper line, so the plain or the sky fills the frame. Use an acacia or a group of animals as your main subject, and keep some open grass around it to show the scale. When you zoom in, hold the phone with both hands and take several shots, because animals move.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the animal on the screen to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright. For a moving animal, try a Live Photo or take a quick burst, then pick the sharpest frame later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The dry season is when wildlife is most concentrated in the park. Within a day, early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and calmer animals.

text.access_note: This is a national park, so entry is likely to be controlled and ticketed; check the official site before you go for entry rules and what visitors may do on foot.

name: Giraffe Centre
label: Giraffe Centre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Giraffe Centre' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Giraffe Centre'.
notes: Feed Rothschild's giraffes from a raised platform.

text.description:
The Giraffe Centre is a wildlife conservation centre in Lang'ata, on the edge of Nairobi, set up to protect the Rothschild's giraffe, a species found only in the grasslands of East Africa. It began in 1979, when Jock Leslie Melville and his wife Betty started a breeding programme on their Lang'ata property, and it opened to visitors by 1983. Its best-known experience is feeding giraffes from a raised platform. Warthogs also wander freely among the giraffes, so keep an eye out for them in the background.

It photographs well because the animals are so tall and so close. From the phone icon on the map, in the lower feeding area of the garden, you can take full-length giraffe portraits with their necks stretching up against the greenery. This is a different angle from the high platform, which gives eye-level shots with a giraffe's head near your phone, often as it takes a pellet. Both are worth trying if you have time. For something more natural, the Gogo River Nature Trail is an alternative, showing giraffes browsing in woodland rather than at a feeding rail.

Step back to fit a whole giraffe in the frame, and let the greenery fill the space around it. Keep your phone strap round your wrist when you are near the animals. The centre is a paid site and the layout of the viewing areas may have changed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Giraffe Centre is in Lang'ata, about 20 kilometres from the centre of Nairobi, on the city's outskirts.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are suitable here, so check current road transport options to Lang'ata, about 20 kilometres from the centre of Nairobi, before you go. The phone icon on the map is about 180 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for full-body giraffe portraits without getting in the animals' way. Use the default lens (1x) to include the garden around them. The ultra-wide (0.5x) works only for a very close head-and-neck shot, and it can stretch the giraffe's shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 180 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The lower garden is where you can fit a whole giraffe in the frame, with its neck stretching up against the greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the giraffe's body on one line, leaving room above its head so the neck does not look cut off. Shoot upwards a little to show the full height against the leaves. If you have time, take a second set from the raised platform for close, eye-level portraits. The Gogo River Nature Trail is a different option, with giraffes in a natural setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the giraffe's face to set focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the animal does not turn into a silhouette. Portrait mode works well when a giraffe is close. Live Photos can catch the moment when one takes a pellet.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light is soft and avoids the harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The Giraffe Centre is a paid, ticketed site; check the official site before you go for entry details and current conditions.
claims_not_in_sources: Giraffes often come close to visitors when pellets are offered, giving a chance for close-up shots.
The ultra-wide lens can distort or stretch the subject when used up close.
A second platform may keep visitors further from the giraffes, so the lower-area and close-up angles may be more limited than older guides describe.

name: Kenyatta International Convention Centre
label: KICC
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'City Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'City Square sublocation' (relation/16328846): edge nearest the subject (2279 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21279654: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kenyatta International Convention Centre' (200 m across).
notes: Iconic cylindrical tower in the city centre.

text.description:
The Kenyatta International Convention Centre, locally known as the KICC, is a 32-storey landmark of Nairobi's city centre. Its main tower is a tall round drum of just over 105 metres, built from simple solid shapes. The amphitheatre and helipad are cone-shaped, and the light terracotta finish is meant to echo traditional African architecture. President Jomo Kenyatta commissioned it in 1967, and it was finished in 1973. For years it was the tallest building in Kenya, and it is still often used as a symbol of Nairobi.

It photographs well because the textured concrete drum is bold, simple and easy to read, even on a small screen. From the closer plaza in front of the main tower entrance, the drum can fill the frame, with flower beds and flagpoles in front of it. That gives you depth without any fuss. The tower's texture looks richest when the afternoon light falls on it.

If you want the tower in its wider setting, Uhuru Park shows it with the downtown skyline behind. On clear mornings you may also see the Ngong Hills far off to the south-west. The rooftop viewing deck gives a 360-degree look over the city centre, but it is a separate, paid option and can close at short notice, so check before you set your plans around it.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Nairobi's city centre (the CBD), on City Square just off Harambee Avenue.
text.directions_text: Aim for the central business district of Nairobi, by taxi, and ask for City Square off Harambee Avenue. The entrance plaza off Harambee Avenue is the closer viewpoint. Roads around the building can be closed at short notice during big events, so a drop-off a little way off may be easier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From where you stand, about 400 m away, use 1x or 2x so the tower sits as a distant landmark in the frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only at the close plaza, when you are near and the drum will not fit. Use the telephoto (3x-5x) only if you want a tight shot of the concrete texture or the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in City Square (plaza in front of the main tower entrance, off Harambee Avenue). The round, concrete drum of the tower filling the frame, with its flower-bed planting and flagpoles in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the drum up with the vertical lines. At the close plaza, put the flower beds or flagpoles along the bottom of the frame to give the picture depth. Try one upright shot to show the full height and one wide shot to show the plaza. For a different view, Uhuru Park shows the tower with the downtown skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the concrete to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the texture stays visible and the sky does not wash out. Keep the phone as level as you can. Tilting it up makes the sides of the tower lean inwards, and the ultra-wide lens makes this stronger.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon, when the light catches the textured concrete. For the Uhuru Park view, a clear morning gives you the best chance of seeing the Ngong Hills.

text.access_note: The plaza is at street level and needs no ticket, but the rooftop deck is a paid, separately run viewing option that can close without notice, so check the news the day before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes the sides of a tall building lean inwards, and the ultra-wide lens makes this stronger.
Roads around the building can be closed at short notice during big events, so a drop-off a little way off may be easier.

name: Karen Blixen Museum
label: Karen Blixen Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karen Blixen Museum' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W509224486 (Karen Blixen Museum): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Farmhouse of the author of Out of Africa.

text.description:
Karen Blixen Museum is a farmhouse with a wide lawn, mature trees and a view across to the Ngong Hills. One guide recommends the back lawn for a frame of the house and hills. There the house is seen from the rear, with the Ngong Hills rising behind the lawn and plenty of green in the foreground.

There are a few other pictures worth taking while you are there. The veranda makes a natural frame, with the lawn and hills seen through it. The garden paths, tall trees and the red-tiled roofline of the farmhouse suit slower, more detailed shots, and if the jacaranda trees are in blossom they add a splash of colour.

For your phone, start with the default lens (1x) and the gridlines switched on, so the roofline and the horizon of the hills sit level. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole house and lawn in one picture, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the hills closer. Keep to the outdoor viewpoints. Rules on photographing inside the house seem to vary, so ask a member of staff on arrival and don't assume flash or indoor shooting is allowed.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Nairobi, with the Ngong Hills rising beyond its back lawn.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Use your map app to navigate to the museum. Once inside the grounds, follow the paths round to the back lawn of the house. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the house and lawn. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the lawn and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Ngong Hills closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, head to the back lawn of the house and look toward the hills, which rise behind the lawn. Turn around to see the house from the rear. For a second angle, stand on the farmhouse veranda and use it as a frame for the lawn and hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines. When shooting the house, put the roofline on the upper third line, and when looking toward the hills, let the lawn and hills fill the frame. Keep the phone level so the house doesn't lean. For a different picture, walk the garden paths and shoot the red-tiled roofline between the mature trees. If the jacaranda is in bloom, use the blossom as a foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hills to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try panorama for the full sweep of the lawn, or a Live Photo if the trees are moving in the breeze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun is behind you as you look toward the hills, according to one guide.

text.access_note: The grounds and house may have different entry arrangements and fees, and opening hours can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bomas of Kenya
label: Bomas of Kenya
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1019332898: the OpenStreetMap point 'Bomas of Kenya'.
notes: Traditional homesteads and cultural dance shows.

text.description: Bomas of Kenya is a cultural village in Langata, Nairobi. 'Bomas' means homesteads, and the site was set up to show traditional homes of several Kenyan communities. The huts are built of mud, thatched grass and wood, so the shapes and textures give you plenty to photograph: round walls, steep thatched roofs and earthen tones against the green of the grounds. The site also has one of the largest auditoriums in Africa, a large structure that suits a wide frame. It opened in October 1971, near Nairobi National Park, and it sits roughly 10 km from the city centre. It is also known for the national constitutional conference held here in 2003 and 2004, and for the Bomas Harambee Dancers, who have performed here since 1973. Bomas was temporarily closed in March 2025 for a major renovation, with a new convention centre planned, so the scene may look different from older pictures. Walk a few steps to either side to keep fences and parked vehicles out of the frame. Wait for a moment with no people crossing in front if you want a clean image. Zoom in for close shots of roof texture rather than walking up to the buildings.
text.geographic_location: Bomas of Kenya is in Langata, Nairobi, close to Nairobi National Park and about 10 km from the city centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed nearby, so travel to Langata. That is about 4 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof thatch and building details. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to a large structure and want to fit it all in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Millennium Hall. A wide frame of the large auditorium with dancers mid-performance and the audience seating visible. The site is to the west, so you look back across the distance toward it. After the first time, treat this point as your base and step a little left or right to find the clearest line of sight.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the roofline on the upper third. Use the 1x lens for the overall view, then zoom to 2x or more to pick out a hut or the shape of the main building. Keep the horizon level. Use foreground grass or a path to add depth, and avoid cutting the top off the roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roofs to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. If people walk through the scene, a Live Photo lets you pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning and late afternoon give softer light and gentler shadows on the thatch and walls. In the morning the sun is behind you, so the site is lit from the front. Around midday the light is harsh and flat.

text.access_note: Bomas of Kenya is a managed visitor site that was temporarily closed for renovation in March 2025, so check the official site before you go for current access and any ticket rules.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, looking west, the morning sun is behind the photographer and lights the site from the front.
Fences, trees or vehicles may partly block the view from the stand-here point.
Midday light in Nairobi is harsh and flat, and morning and late afternoon light is softer.

name: Nairobi National Museum
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Great Court' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Great Court' (way/79622541): middle (126 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/95122002: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nairobi National Museum' (75 m across).
notes: Kenya's main museum of nature, history and culture.

text.description: Nairobi National Museum sits on Museum Hill, in leafy grounds between the city centre and Westlands. It began in 1910 as a natural history society's collection. It opened as the Coryndon Museum in 1930, took its present name in 1964 after independence, and reopened in June 2008 after a major rebuild. For a phone photo, the best-known view is from the open courtyard in front of the building, which one guide calls the Great Court. From the courtyard the front facade and its architecture sit neatly across the open space, and early morning or late afternoon light gives longer shadows and more shape to the walls. Two other spots are worth a look. One is the entrance gate on Museum Hill Road, with its mosaic-tiled pillars and white archway and greenery behind. The other is the Botanic Garden within the museum grounds, where the museum building can sit in the background of a lawn or garden shot. Stand back far enough to fit the whole front in the frame, and keep the sun behind or beside you rather than in front of the lens. Inside, photography is generally allowed in most galleries without flash, but ask staff if you are unsure.
text.geographic_location: On Museum Hill in Nairobi, close to Uhuru Highway, between the Central Business District and Westlands. The museum shares its grounds with the Snake Park and the Botanic Garden.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach Museum Hill from the city centre or Westlands. The courtyard viewpoint, which one guide calls the Great Court, is in front of the building, so look for it once you are in the grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough, and keep the building centred so the edges don't stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Great Court (open courtyard in front of the museum building). The museum's front facade and architecture framed across the open courtyard, best shot in early morning or late afternoon light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with them so the walls stand straight. Keep some courtyard in the foreground to give a sense of space. For a second shot, try the decorative gate on Museum Hill Road, with its mosaic-tiled pillars and white archway and greenery behind. The Botanic Garden within the museum grounds is another option, with the museum as a backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the facade keeps its detail. Take a few shots as you move, because low sun changes the shadows quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the low sun adds shadow and depth to the facade.

text.access_note: The grounds and galleries may be ticketed and photography rules can vary (commercial shoots need permission), so check the official site before you go.

name: Uhuru Park
label: Uhuru Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Uhuru Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Uhuru Park' (way/4742143): edge nearest the subject (861 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4742143: large area 'Uhuru Park' (865 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large central park with a lake and the Nyayo monument.

text.description: Uhuru Park is a 12.9 hectare (32 acre) green space right beside Nairobi's central business district. It opened to the public on 23 May 1969 and has an artificial lake, several national monuments and a large open assembly ground. For a phone photo the lake is the draw. Stand at the water's edge and the city skyline rises behind the trees, so you get green foreground, water and towers in one frame. When the water is calm it can mirror the trees too. The park closed in November 2021 and reopened on 30 March 2024 after renovation, so some features may have changed since older photos were taken. Keep the horizon level using gridlines, and let the lake take up the lower third of the picture. Tap on the skyline to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. If you have time, there is a second view looking back across the park towards the KICC tower, and the lawns have wildlife sculptures such as warthogs and rhinos that make a fun foreground. Go early, ideally before 9:00 AM, when the light is softer and it is quieter. Plan to leave before dusk, as the area is reported to be less safe after dark.
text.geographic_location: Uhuru Park lies right beside Nairobi's central business district. From the lakeside the city's towers form the skyline behind.
text.directions_text: Head for the central business district and then to Uhuru Park. Once in the park, follow the paths towards the lake. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lake with the skyline behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more water and sky, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer and make them feel bigger behind the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Uhuru Park (lakeside, with the skyline behind). The park's man-made lake with the Nairobi skyline in the background, sometimes reflecting trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the water in the lower third and the skyline along the upper third, with a tree or two at one edge to frame the picture. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon straight. If you want a person in the shot, ask them to stand at the water's edge with the skyline behind them and use portrait mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo to catch ripples or people moving by the lake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9:00 AM, for the softest light and the fewest people. Leave before dusk.

text.access_note: The park reopened in 2024 and entry is reported as free with a national ID; check the official site for current entry and photography rules before you go, as professional shoots need a permit.

name: Jamia Mosque (Kenya)
label: Jamia Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Banda Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Banda Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/140320795: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jamia Mosque' (150 m across).
notes: Large white mosque with green domes.

text.description:
Jamia Mosque is a Sunni mosque in central Nairobi that was described as the largest in East Africa when it was completed, and a white façade, twin minarets and three silver domes make it an easy subject for a phone. It stands on Banda Street in the Central Business District. The Glasgow-based architect William Landels designed it, and it was built between 1925 and 1933. Its style borrows mainly from seventeenth-century Mughal mosques, such as the Jama Masjid in Delhi and the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, with some British and Scottish touches. When it was finished in 1933 it was the tallest building in Nairobi. It was paid for by a long community fundraising drive, with gifts from people of many backgrounds across East Africa and India, and it opened on 18 August 1933.

From there you look at the south elevation, the street front of the mosque, straight on, with both minarets and all three domes in one frame. If you want a different view, the front grounds give a closer shot of the domes and minarets with the courtyard and entrance in the foreground. Kenyatta Avenue gives a more distant street-level view that includes the neighbouring library block, in the manner of older Nairobi photographs. Stay on the street or in the open grounds, and ask before photographing anyone at prayer.
text.geographic_location: Jamia Mosque is on Banda Street in Nairobi's Central Business District, south of the old Indian markets area. It sits among the busy streets of the city centre.
text.directions_text: Head for Banda Street in the Central Business District. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on façade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the minarets are cut off. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes and minaret tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Banda Street (south elevation, facing the mosque's street façade). The white façade with its twin minarets and three silver domes, seen straight on from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the minarets with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep your phone level and as upright as you can. Include the whole front with a little sky above the domes. For a closer view, try the front grounds of the mosque. For a more distant, street-level view, try Kenyatta Avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the walls stay bright but keep their detail and the silver domes do not blow out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a weekday, early or late in the day, for a clearer front view. Friday prayers bring crowds, so it is best to avoid them.

text.access_note: Jamia Mosque is a working place of worship, so respect prayer times, ask permission before taking any photos inside, and check opening and prayer times locally before you go.

name: Parliament Buildings (Kenya)
label: Parliament Buildings
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Uhuru Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Uhuru Park' (way/4742143): edge nearest the subject (861 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3224460: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kenya Parliament Buildings' (173 m across).
notes: Seat of the Kenyan legislature with its clock tower.

text.description:
The Parliament Buildings are the seat of Kenya's Parliament, and the clock tower is the part that stands out in a photo. The complex was built in 1954 for the colonial Legislative Council and was known as the Legislative Buildings until 1963. It was designed by Amyas Connell and Harold Thornley Dyer, and the English-style clock tower was a design requirement so that the buildings would echo the Palace of Westminster and Big Ben. Kenya's first president, Jomo Kenyatta, is buried on the estate.

The clock tower is visible from Uhuru Park, the free public park across from the complex. From the lakeside the tower rises above the artificial lake, with the city skyline behind it. That gives you water, tower and skyline in a single frame. Parliament Road, beside the buildings, is an alternative for a long street view along the complex.

Keep your photos to the park and the public road. This is a working government complex with security, so don't walk up to the buildings to get closer. A steady 1x shot with the lake in the lower third works well, and a zoom shot picks out the tower. Take a few frames, as people and joggers wander through the park and you may want a clear one.
text.geographic_location: In central Nairobi, at the Parliament Buildings, directly across from Uhuru Park and its artificial lake.
text.directions_text: Head to Uhuru Park in central Nairobi, the public park across from the Parliament complex. From there the Parliament Buildings are to the east, and the clock tower is the part to look for. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the lake, the tower and the skyline together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the clock tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of lake and sky, as the tower will look small and buildings at the edges may lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Uhuru Park (lakeside, facing west toward the building). The Parliament clock tower rising above the artificial lake, with the city skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Put the water in the lower third and the tower slightly off-centre, leaving the skyline visible behind it. For a different angle, try a long street view along Parliament Road beside the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the clock tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a couple of frames in a row, because people and joggers may walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or later afternoon usually gives softer light than the middle of the day. In the afternoon the sun will be roughly behind you when you face east.

text.access_note: Uhuru Park is a free public park, but Parliament is a working government complex, so stay in the park or on the public road and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Parliament is a working government complex with security, and photographing from closer than the public road or park edge may be restricted.
Uhuru Park is a free public park directly across from the Parliament complex.
People and joggers may walk through the lakeside area of Uhuru Park.
Morning or later afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
In the afternoon the sun is roughly behind a photographer facing east.

name: Nairobi Arboretum
label: Nairobi Arboretum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arboretum Drive' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Arboretum Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Green park with many tree species.

text.description: Nairobi Arboretum is a large, leafy park in Kilimani, laid out for trees rather than for show, and that is why it photographs well. Trunks, branches and canopy close in around you and make natural frames, and a phone copes well with that kind of soft green scene. It was founded in 1907 by Mr. Batiscombe, who wanted to try out new forestry trees, and it was gazetted as a national reserve in 1932. The best first picture is at the main gate on Arboretum Drive, by the entrance near Kenya Girl Guides Headquarters. From there you can look straight into the tree-lined grounds, with the trunks and canopy leading the eye inwards. Once inside, two further pictures are worth looking for. One is the large fig tree, which makes a strong central subject when its spreading canopy fills the frame. The other is the bamboo section, where tall culms rise out of the top of the picture and show the scale of the place. Walk in from the main gate and look for the central fig tree and the bamboo stand. Paths can be muddy in places and there are monkeys, so keep your phone and snacks secure and do not feed them. Early morning or late afternoon gives the softest light under the trees.
text.geographic_location: Nairobi Arboretum is in the Kilimani area of Nairobi, along State House Road. The main gate is on Arboretum Drive, near Kenya Girl Guides Headquarters.
text.directions_text: Ask for the Arboretum main gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate view, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the fig tree's canopy and the tall bamboo. Use telephoto (2x-5x) if you want to pick out a detail in the branches without leaving the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Arboretum Drive (at the main gate, by the entrance near Kenya Girl Guides Headquarters). A framed view from the entrance looking into the tree-lined grounds, with the trunks and canopy leading the eye inward. At the gate, look into the grounds, where the trunks and canopy lead the eye inward along the line of trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the entrance path or the line of trunks on the centre line, so the trees frame the picture on both sides. Inside the park, for the large fig tree, step back until the spreading canopy fills the frame. For the bamboo, hold the phone low and tilt it up so the culms run out of the top of the picture and show the scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest trunk to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sunlit patches do not wash out. Portrait mode works well for a person standing in front of the fig tree.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: This is a park with a main gate, and photography charges or permits may apply, particularly for formal or commercial shoots, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nairobi Gallery
label: Nairobi Gallery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway (our map tiles).

notes: Colonial-era building used as an art gallery.

text.description: Nairobi Gallery is a handsome colonial-era building at the edge of Nairobi's central business district, and its exterior is the reason to bring your phone. Seen from the pavement at the junction of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway, the old stonework stands against the tall, modern office towers of the city centre. That mix of old and new is what makes the picture. The building was designed by C. Rand Ovary and finished in 1913 as a government office. It was declared a national monument in 1995 and passed to the National Museums of Kenya in 1997. After renovation it opened as a gallery in 2005, and it now shows African art. Inside there are pan-African stamps, jewellery, textiles, carvings, paintings, and furniture and photographs from Joseph Murumbi's collection. The building is about 49 metres across, so you will need to step back a little to fit the whole front into the frame. Start with a wide shot of the facade and the skyline behind it. Then move closer for details such as the doorway, windows and rooflines. Point Zero is a recommended second picture, with the marker in the foreground and the gallery behind it. Check the map for the distance. The junction is a working city corner, so expect people and vehicles in your shots. Take a few frames and pick the cleanest one.
text.geographic_location: Nairobi Gallery stands at the edge of Nairobi's central business district, at the junction of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot, so use the map to reach the junction of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and some skyline from the pavement. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched look. Use 2x or 3x on the telephoto for details such as the doorway or windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway (junction where the gallery stands; frame the building's exterior from the pavement). The colonial-era exterior of the gallery set against the modern skyscrapers of central Nairobi. The gallery is to the east of you. Check the exact pavement position on the map.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges parallel to them, so the walls do not lean. Place the gallery on one side of the grid and let the skyscrapers fill the other. For a second picture, go to Point Zero and put the marker in the foreground with the historic facade behind it. Check the map for the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots, because people and traffic pass through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the facade than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public pavement; for visiting the galleries inside, and for any photography rules there, check the official site before you go.

name: All Saints' Cathedral, Nairobi
label: All Saints Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kenyatta Avenue' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kenyatta Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description:
All Saints' Cathedral is the Anglican cathedral in the middle of Nairobi, and it is a good subject for a straightforward, tidy exterior photo. It is a solid stone church with a strong street-facing front. It sits close to Uhuru Park, so there is usually some open space and greenery around it.

The building has a long history. A public meeting in 1914 raised money for a permanent church in the city centre. The architect was Temple Moore, and the foundation stone was laid on 3 February 1917. It became the Cathedral of the Highlands in 1924 and was finally consecrated in 1952, after more sections were added in 1934 and 1952. The cathedral also has a place in Kenya's modern history: in the early 1990s, mothers of political prisoners held a long vigil here, and the prisoners were released in early 1993.

The best photo is the front of the cathedral from the public pavement on Kenyatta Avenue, opposite the Nairobi Serena Hotel. Keep to exterior pictures: photography inside is restricted and needs permission. On Sundays, services bring crowds and security queues near the building, so a weekday is easier if you want a clear view.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in central Nairobi, on Kenyatta Avenue next to Uhuru Park. It is within easy reach of the city centre.
text.directions_text: Head for central Nairobi and then to Kenyatta Avenue, beside Uhuru Park. By taxi or on foot, ask for All Saints' Cathedral on Kenyatta Avenue. From there, walk to the public pavement opposite the Nairobi Serena Hotel, where you can see the cathedral front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: For a fuller view of the front, walk to the pavement directly opposite the cathedral front and then use the default lens (1x). Use the telephoto for details such as the stonework and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kenyatta Avenue (public pavement opposite Nairobi Serena Hotel, facing the cathedral front). The cathedral's street-facing front, shot from the sidewalk across the wide Kenyatta Avenue carriageway. If you are not already there, walk to it. Face the cathedral's street-facing front, which lies to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the front with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and include a little pavement or greenery at the bottom for scale. Wait for a gap in the traffic and people to keep the foreground clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral front to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case a vehicle passes through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A weekday is calmer than Sunday, when services bring crowds and security queues. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light.

text.access_note: You can photograph the exterior from the public pavement on Kenyatta Avenue; this is a place of worship, so keep to exterior shots, ask permission before photographing inside and check the official site before you go.

name: Nairobi Railway Museum
label: Railway Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Station Road' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/991475260: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nairobi Railway Museum' (244 m across).
notes: Historic steam locomotives of the Kenya-Uganda railway.

text.description:
The Nairobi Railway Museum sits right beside Nairobi railway station and is run by Kenya Railways. It opened in 1971 and keeps exhibits from the old East African Railways, including early diesel locomotives, passenger coaches and a small working miniature railway added in 2011. The star for many visitors is locomotive 301, a preserved steam engine that appeared in the 1985 film Out of Africa.

For a phone photographer, the museum works on two levels. Inside, the phone icon on the map is at the centre of the museum site, and the open-air yard around it gives you rows of locomotives with plenty of colour, rust and texture. Outside, another viewpoint is the jacaranda-lined road that leads from the station towards the museum entrance, which may be called Station Road (please verify the name and exact spot on the map). In the jacaranda season the trees make a soft, purple-toned frame, with the station and the museum's trees behind. It is a possible alternative to shooting only the trains, and it is probably reachable from outside the museum, but check the road on the map first.

Start at the phone icon on the map and work around the yard, looking for locomotive 301 against the rail yard and its other locomotives. If you also want the road view, walk slowly towards the museum gate and shoot as you go, keeping the road running into the picture so the trees lead the eye. Personal phone photography is generally allowed, but check the official site before you go, especially if you plan anything more elaborate.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Nairobi, Kenya, immediately next to Nairobi railway station. A jacaranda-lined road leads from the station towards the museum entrance; verify the name 'Station Road' and its exact position on the map.
text.directions_text: Make for Nairobi railway station, which the museum sits right beside. Check a map app for the best way to reach the railway station from where you are. The phone icon on the map is at the centre of the museum site, so head for the museum entrance. If you want the road view, look for the tree-lined road between the station and the museum gate and confirm it on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the locomotives and, if you try the road view, the trees. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want a whole locomotive, or the whole avenue and the station in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to compress the tree-lined road, or to pick out a locomotive or station detail from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. As an alternative viewpoint, try the jacaranda-lined road outside the station (possibly called Station Road), with the museum's trees and the railway station in the background. Check its position on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines. For the road view, place the road on a line so the trees form a tunnel leading to the gate, and keep the phone level so the verticals of the trunks stay straight. Inside the museum grounds, locomotive 301, the steam engine from Out of Africa, looks good against the open-air rail yard and its other locomotives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on a locomotive, the road or the nearest tree, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the blossom keep their colour. Take a few shots as you walk, in case a passer-by steps into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: September and October, when the jacarandas are in bloom, if you want the road view. Outside those months the road may still be a pleasant, shaded approach, and soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The museum viewpoints, including the stand-here point inside the site, require an entry ticket, and professional or tripod shoots may need a booking, so check the official site before you go. The road view outside is unconfirmed, so verify it on the map.

name: Jeevanjee Gardens
label: Jeevanjee Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Moi Avenue' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Moi Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/123416385: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jeevanjee Gardens' (251 m across).
notes: Small city park in the downtown area.

text.description:
Jeevanjee Gardens is a green, open park in the middle of Nairobi's Central Business District. It was founded by A.M. Jeevanjee, an Asian-born entrepreneur in Kenya, who gave it to the people of Nairobi as a resting place. It was private property and is held in trust for the public. It is described as the only park in the city owned directly by the people, which is a nice detail to mention if you post the photo.

The best view for a phone is from the Moi Avenue side, looking in from the eastern entrance. Looking in from the gate, you see the mature trees and the paved walkways leading inside, so the paths pull the eye into the picture and the branches frame the top. If you want a second picture, the statue of Alibhai Mulla Jeevanjee stands among the shade trees and benches further in. Skip the old Queen Victoria monument, because only its pedestal remains.

If people are in your shot, keep them small and incidental. Some visitors come for the open-air debates held here, but it is polite not to point your phone at individuals. The park may have building or repair work going on, so check for current works before you plan your visit.
text.geographic_location: Jeevanjee Gardens is an open garden in Nairobi's Central Business District. The photo spot is on the Moi Avenue side of the park, on its eastern side, about 75 m north-east of the middle of the gardens.
text.directions_text: Start from the Central Business District in central Nairobi and go by road or on foot to the Moi Avenue side of the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the entrance, trees and paths look natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the walkways and tree canopy, and use 2x for the statue or distant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Moi Avenue (at the eastern entrance to the park, looking in along the paths). The park's main entrance framed by its mature trees and the paved walkways leading inside. The gardens spread out to the south-west from here, and you should see the main gate framed by mature trees and paved walkways leading inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the main path along one of the lines so it leads the eye into the park. Let the tree branches fill the top of the frame. Keep the phone level so the gate and path edges stay straight. If you also visit the statue of Alibhai Mulla Jeevanjee, use 2x and include the benches and shade trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the shaded path to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky behind the trees looks washed out. Check that the lens is clean before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: The gardens are an open public park, but works may be under way, so check local information before you go.
